source.title: Understanding Instance-Level Label Noise: Disparate Impacts and Treatments

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes noisy-label memorization theoretically and reports a CIFAR-10 experiment using loss distributions, a different measure from the claim versions’ training and test errors.
record.gate_note: The CIFAR-10 experiment reports that the network fails to separate clean from corrupted instances and memorizes a mixture. This does not measure fitting fully random labels, training error, test error, optimization time, or the other listed version outcomes. Figure 2’s toy illustration and other cited results are not extracted as results for a claim version.
record.test_reason: The theoretical results condition on a model memorizing the empirical noisy-label distribution. They quantify consequences and correction methods rather than establish any listed version. Figure 3 measures clean/noisy loss-distribution overlap, without establishing perfect fit, chance test performance, optimization time, or clean-before-noisy learning.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. More precisely, the conditional theory gives frequency-dependent bounds on generalization harm and shows that loss correction and peer loss can improve predictions with high probability for frequent instances while worsening predictions with substantial probability for rare instances.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a CIFAR-10 ResNet-34 experiment with synthesized instance-independent and instance-dependent noise, and theoretically analyzes noisy-label memorization. It does not reproduce the original completely random-label experiment or its error measures.

fits_no_version.finding: For both synthesized instance-independent and instance-dependent noise on CIFAR-10, the authors report overlapping clean/corrupted loss distributions and memorization of a mixture.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the tested conditions, ResNet-34's normalized training losses do not cleanly distinguish clean examples from corrupted examples.

fits_no_version.finding: Conditional on the paper's definition of noisy-label memorization, its theory bounds instance-level generalization harm and shows that correction methods can fail with substantial probability for rare instances.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The generalization consequences of memorizing noisy labels and the reliability of noise correction depend on instance frequency.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 139, 2021
record.problems: The experiment is reported through loss-distribution plots and a qualitative description, without numeric fit or generalization errors in the supplied text. The text defers empirical details to the appendix and does not give the noise rates for Figure 3 in the supplied passage.
record.rows_left_out: No other rows bear on the listed versions. Figure 2 and Figure 5 are toy 2D illustrations; the text describes their predicted probabilities but they do not measure a listed version’s fit or generalization outcome. Figure 4 concerns peer loss. Results cited from other studies are not extracted.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error and chance test error under completely random labeling, with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true and random labels, and convergence slowdown across corruption fractions.
Perfect training fit on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit and steadily increasing test error across corruption fractions from zero to complete corruption. The conditional generalization bound does not establish this empirical trajectory.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Whether shared real-data patterns are learned before noisy labels. Figure 3 shows distributions across epochs but supplies no stated result establishing or contradicting that ordering.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's memorization definition matches randomized predictions to an empirical label distribution; it is not a demonstration of zero training classification error. The toy examples and mitigation results do not supply missing tests of the listed versions.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test completely random labeling, training error, test error, or whether architecture and training hyperparameters remain unchanged.
The study does not compare training time or convergence across corruption rates.
The study does not train on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
The CIFAR-10 experiment examines loss distributions under noisy labels but does not report perfect training fit or test error across a sweep from no corruption to complete corruption.
The study does not test whether regularization or augmentation prevents fitting random labels, or whether their removal harms generalization on true labels.
The study does not test the ordering or difference of learning real and random labels over training; its citation of Arpit et al. is prior work.

rows.subject: ResNet-34
rows.operation_detail: Compared the training-loss distributions of clean and corrupted CIFAR-10 instances across training epochs under synthesized label noise.

conditions.value: simple instance-independent noise and instance-dependent noise

rows.measure: Separation of clean-instance and corrupted-instance loss distributions; the authors report that the network fails to separate them and memorizes a mixture.
rows.value: The neural network fails to separate clean instances from corrupted ones and memorizes a mixture of both.
rows.locator: Section 3.4, Figure 3; Appendix B, Details for generating Figure 3
rows.note: The text reports the qualitative loss-distribution result, but this measure does not establish the training error, test error, or outcomes across the corruption sweep specified in V4. Appendix B states the ResNet-34 training setup.
rows.check: The qualitative finding is accurately paraphrased, but overlapping loss distributions do not establish any listed version, including V6's learning order. The Figure 3 discussion is in Section 3.3, rather than Section 3.4. The plotted measure is normalized cross-entropy loss, which can be negative, rather than raw training loss. The two noise conditions should ideally be separate rows.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
